svg.aria-label: Diagram: Azure deployment stacks and managed resources, showing that the stack holds the record of what it manages so Azure keeps it rather than you, the actionOnUnmanage matrix of detachAll deleteResources and deleteAll, the difference between a managed and a detached resource, the limits of 800 stacks and 2000 deny assignments per scope, and four documented failure modes including the stack-out-of-sync error, resource group deletion bypassing deny assignments, a move stripping stack protection, and what-if not being supported
svg.title: A deployment stack keeps the record of what it manages, so Azure holds it instead of you — and the record has its own failure modes
svg.text: Terraform hands you a record to keep. A deployment stack keeps one for you.
Same idea, opposite custody — no file, no lock, no backend to bootstrap. And no preview, because what-if is not supported.
Managed
In the template, and in the stack’s resource list.
"status": "managed", "denyStatus": "none"
Add one by adding it to the Bicep file and updating
the stack. Remove one by deleting it from the file
and updating the stack.
The template is the whole interface to the list.
Detached
A resource the stack no longer tracks or manages,
but which still exists in Azure.
Detaching is the default.
Stacks detach rather than delete unmanaged resources
unless told otherwise — the safe direction, and the
reason orphans accumulate quietly.
actionOnUnmanage — what happens to anything that leaves the list
detachAll
leave the resources and the resource groups in place — the default
deleteResources
delete the resources, keep the resource groups
deleteAll
delete both — and a deleted resource group takes everything inside it,
including resources the stack never managed
One exception runs the other way: unmanaged resources in the stack’s own resource group stop that group being deleted at all.
Four documented ways the record and reality come apart
1 · The list goes out of sync
The stack “might not have an accurate list of managed
resources”. Review it, redeploy the same template, and
only then pass BypassStackOutOfSyncError.
Do not use that switch by default: it is the one that
turns an uncertain list into a delete.
2 · Deleting the resource group wins
A stack at resource group scope does not manage its own
parent group, because the group is not in the Bicep file.
So the group can still be deleted — taking the stack and
every resource it protected with it.
Fix: deploy at subscription scope, group in the file.
3 · A move strips the protection
Deny assignments are evaluated at resource group scope
for Move, not at the resource. So a protected resource can
be moved out, and the protection does not travel with it.
Interim mitigation: a ReadOnly lock on the group. Stack
reads and deny-delete keep working under it.
4 · The preview is newer than the docs
The known issues page says what-if is unsupported.
A page dated 12 August 2026 documents it in full, and
it reports what would be detached or deleted. Believe
the newer, more specific page.
Limits per scope: 800 deployment stacks, and 2,000 deny assignments — two and a half deny assignments per stack if both are reached.
Not managed at all: implicitly created resources, so no deny assignment and no cleanup for them. Deny assignments do not support
tags, are unsupported at management group scope, and a stack cannot delete Key Vault secrets — remove those in detach mode.
Sources: Create and deploy Azure deployment stacks in Bicep, and Known issues for deployment stacks, on Microsoft Learn.
